Question:
The number of ordered pairs of integers \((m, n)\) for which \(mn \ge 0\) and

\[m^3 + n^3 + 99mn = 33^3\]

is equal to
Solution:
The coefficient \(99=3\cdot33\) suggests comparing the expression with the cube of \(m+n\). Set \(s=m+n\) and \(p=mn\). Expanding \((m+n)^3\) gives \(m^3+n^3=s^3-3ps\), so the equation becomes
\[
s^3-33^3-3p(s-33)=0.
\]
Factoring the difference of cubes yields
\[
(s-33)(s^2+33s+1089-3p)=0.
\]
Write the second factor as \(Q\). In terms of \(m,n\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
Q&=m^2+n^2-mn+33m+33n+1089\\
&=\frac{(m-n)^2+(m+33)^2+(n+33)^2}{2}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This sum of nonnegative squares makes the second case easy to resolve. The original equation is equivalent to one of the following two cases.

If \(s=33\), then \(n=33-m\). The condition \(mn\geq0\) becomes \(m(33-m)\geq0\), which holds exactly when \(0\leq m\leq33\). Each of the \(34\) integers \(m=0,1,\ldots,33\) determines one different ordered pair \((m,33-m)\), including both zero-product endpoints.

If \(Q=0\), every square in its displayed expression must be zero. Thus \(m=n=-33\). This pair has positive product and satisfies the factored equation, hence the original equation. Its sum is \(-66\), so it was not counted in the first case.

The factorization exhausts all possibilities, and the two counted cases are disjoint. The number of ordered pairs is therefore \(\boxed{34+1=35}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
